nodes.summary: The set of all clauses of at most $k$ literals over $t$ variables. Its conjunction is the initial hypothesis of the elimination algorithm.
nodes.title: Clauses of at most $k$ literals

nodes.summary: There are at most $\sum_{j=0}^{k} (2t)^j$ clauses of at most $k$ literals over $t$ variables: there are $2t$ literals, hence at most $\binom{2t}{j} \le (2t)^j$ clauses of exactly $j$ literals. Valiant counts the clauses of one to $k$ literals as fewer than $(2t)^{k+1}$; the sum here also counts the empty clause.
nodes.title: Counting the initial clauses

nodes.summary: The class of $k$-CNF functions over $t$ variables has at most $2^N$ members, where $N$ is the number of clauses of at most $k$ literals.
nodes.title: Size of the k-CNF class

nodes.summary: A clause is a finite set of literals, read as their disjunction (Valiant's "sum of literals").
nodes.title: Clause

nodes.summary: A conjunctive normal form (CNF) expression is a finite set of clauses, read as their conjunction (Valiant's "product of clauses").
nodes.title: CNF expression

nodes.summary: If $f$ is a $k$-CNF expression satisfied by every example, then at every assignment where the elimination output is true, $f$ is true. This is condition (i) of Valiant's definition of learnability: the hypothesis "never outputs one when it should not".
nodes.title: One-sided error: the elimination hypothesis implies the target

nodes.summary: The output of elimination is a subset of the clauses of at most $k$ literals.
nodes.title: The elimination output keeps only initial clauses

nodes.summary: Given a list of positive examples (truth assignments at which the target is true), the elimination algorithm starts from all clauses of at most $k$ literals and deletes each clause falsified by some example; it outputs the conjunction of the remaining clauses. Valiant's loop body is "for each $c_i$ in $g$ delete $c_i$ if $v \not\Rightarrow c_i$", repeated over the examples $v$; the result does not depend on the…
nodes.title: Valiant's elimination algorithm for k-CNF

nodes.summary: Every example given to the elimination algorithm satisfies the CNF expression it outputs.
nodes.title: The elimination output is consistent with the positive examples

nodes.summary: A clause is true at an assignment $x$ when one of its literals is true at $x$; the empty clause is true nowhere.
nodes.title: Truth of a clause

nodes.summary: A CNF expression is true at an assignment $x$ when each of its clauses is true at $x$; the empty expression is true everywhere.
nodes.title: Truth of a CNF expression

nodes.summary: The literal $(i, b)$ is true at a truth assignment $x : \{0, \dots, t-1\} \to \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ when $x_i = b$.
nodes.title: Truth of a literal

nodes.summary: On every labelled sample realizable by a $k$-CNF function $f$, the elimination learner outputs a $k$-CNF function that agrees with every label, i.e. it is consistent with the class of $k$-CNF functions in the sense of CSLib's `IsConsistent`: its output is true at the positive examples, which satisfy it, and false at the negative examples, because it implies $f$.
nodes.title: The elimination learner is consistent with the k-CNF class

nodes.summary: Every clause kept by the elimination algorithm has at most $k$ literals.
nodes.title: The elimination output is a k-CNF expression

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$, a CNF expression is a $k$-CNF expression when each of its clauses has at most $k$ literals.
nodes.title: k-CNF expression

nodes.summary: For fixed $t$ and $k$, the class of $k$-CNF functions over $t$ variables is PAC learnable in CSLib's sense (`IsPACLearnable`) over its realizable family, by the elimination learner with $\lceil \log(|\text{k-CNF}| / \delta) / \varepsilon \rceil$ examples. This is the sample-size part of Valiant's Theorem A; the polynomial running time of the algorithm is not formalized.
nodes.title: k-CNF is PAC learnable

nodes.summary: The hypothesis class of $k$-CNF functions over $t$ variables, as a finite set of Boolean functions: the Boolean functions of the subsets of the clauses of at most $k$ literals.
nodes.title: The class of k-CNF functions

nodes.summary: The output of the elimination learner belongs to the class of $k$-CNF functions.
nodes.title: The elimination learner outputs a k-CNF function

nodes.summary: The elimination learner is a CSLib `Learner` on labelled samples of truth assignments: it runs the elimination algorithm on the positive examples of the sample and outputs the Boolean function of the resulting $k$-CNF expression. It reads only the labelled sample, never the target; the negative examples are ignored.
nodes.title: The elimination learner

nodes.summary: A literal over the variables $p_0, \dots, p_{t-1}$ is a pair $(i, b)$ with $i < t$ and $b \in \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$: the variable $p_i$ when $b$ is true and its negation $\bar p_i$ when $b$ is false.
nodes.title: Literal over $t$ Boolean variables

nodes.summary: For a hypothesis $h$ on truth assignments of $t$ variables, the disagreement set $\{(x, y) : h(x) \ne y\}$ is measurable, as is every subset of the finite set of labelled assignments.
nodes.title: Disagreement sets of Boolean hypotheses are measurable

nodes.summary: An assignment is one of the positive examples of a labelled sample exactly when the sample contains it with the label $\mathrm{true}$.
nodes.title: Membership in the positive examples

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be any probability distribution on labelled truth assignments of $t$ Boolean variables under which some $k$-CNF function has error $0$ (the realizable case). For $m$ independent examples from $D$, the probability that the elimination learner outputs a hypothesis whose error exceeds $\varepsilon$ is at most $2^N (1 - \varepsilon)^m$, where $N$ is the number of clauses of at most $k$ literals over the $t$…
nodes.title: k-CNF is PAC learnable by elimination

nodes.summary: The instances of a labelled sample of truth assignments that carry the label $\mathrm{true}$, in sample order.
nodes.title: Positive examples of a labelled sample

nodes.summary: If $f$ is a $k$-CNF expression and every example satisfies $f$, then every clause of $f$ survives elimination. This is the special case, for the clauses of $f$ itself, of Valiant's observation that "in the course of the algorithm no clause in $B$ can ever be deleted", where $B$ is the set of all clauses of at most $k$ literals implied by $f$.
nodes.title: The target's clauses are never deleted

nodes.summary: The Boolean function $x \mapsto [f \text{ is true at } x]$ computed by a CNF expression $f$.
nodes.title: Boolean function of a CNF expression

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
